title: A bison in the grasslands of Theodore Roosevelt National Park, North Dakota, USA
caption: Info
subtitle: A bison in Theodore Roosevelt National Park, USA
description:
Bison are among the largest land mammals in the world, capable of weighing up to 900 kilograms and reaching speeds of 65 kilometres per hour despite their massive size. Despite often being called a buffalo, the American bison is not one of the true buffaloes, which are native to Africa and Asia. Its scientific name, Bison bison, leaves little room for confusion.
Its muscular shoulder hump helps it swing its head side to side, clearing snow to reach grass underneath. Both males and females grow horns and beards. Their tails offer clues about their mood: a swishing tail generally signals calm, while a raised tail may indicate agitation.

title: Flamingos in Ebro Delta Natural Park, Catalonia, Spain
caption: Info
subtitle: Flamingos in Ebro Delta Natural Park, Catalonia, Spain
description: The Ebro Delta in Catalonia is one of Spain's most rewarding places to see flamingos. These unmistakable birds can be spotted throughout the year, often gathering in the delta's shallow lagoons, salt pans and coastal waters. Their long legs let them wade through the water while feeding, while their pink colouring comes from pigments found in their diet. With wetlands, rice fields, beaches and the Mediterranean all meeting here, the delta provides an important home for both resident and migratory birds. Flamingos have become one of its most recognisable sights, adding a splash of colour to this remarkable landscape.

title: Historic district of Triana, Seville, Spain
caption: Info
subtitle: Historic district of Triana, Seville, Spain
description:
Cross the Guadalquivir River in Seville, the capital of Spain's Andalusia region, and the city's rhythm seems to change. On the other side lies Triana, a colourful neighbourhood where ceramics, flamenco and local traditions are woven into everyday life. Since the 19th century, the Isabel II Bridge, also known as the Triana Bridge, has connected the neighbourhood to Seville's historic centre.
Step off the bridge and Triana's distinctive character comes into view. The neighbourhood has a long tradition of pottery and tilemaking, and colourful azulejos still brighten facades and workshops. Its streets have also played an important role in the history of flamenco, an art form deeply associated with Triana. Along Calle Betis, brightly painted buildings face the Guadalquivir.
Triana isn't defined by a single monument. Its appeal lies in its mix of artisans and markets, music and tiled courtyards, riverside terraces and narrow streets. Seville may be just across the water, but Triana has a spirit all its own.

title: Aerial view of Rose Island, The Bahamas
caption: Info
subtitle: Aerial view of Rose Island, The Bahamas
description:
From above, Rose Island looks like a brushstroke of green surrounded by every shade of blue. Just five kilometres east of Paradise Island in The Bahamas, this slender cay trades busy roads and city blocks for sandy shores, shallow waters and an inland lagoon. Its peaceful appearance comes with a touch of movie drama. Rose Island was used as a filming location for the 1965 James Bond adventure 'Thunderball', including the explosive destruction of the Disco Volante.
Beyond its cinematic cameo, Rose Island offers a glimpse of what makes The Bahamas so striking. The island is known for its swimming pigs, adding an unexpected touch of character to its shores. Across the archipelago, low-lying islands and cays meet reefs, sandbars and brilliant shallows. Pale sand beneath clear water creates ribbons of turquoise, aquamarine and deep blue. From this height, land and sea seem to blur together, proving that sometimes the best view of paradise comes from above.

title: The Atlantic Forest, Brazil
caption: Info
subtitle: The Atlantic Forest, Brazil
description: The Atlantic Forest is one of the world's great biodiversity hotspots, stretching along much of Brazil's Atlantic coast and into Argentina and Paraguay. Its landscape includes tropical and subtropical forests, mangroves and coastal habitats, providing a home for around 20,000 plant species and an extraordinary variety of wildlife, including jaguars and golden lion tamarins. Much of the forest has disappeared over the centuries, but it continues to play an important role in storing carbon and providing fresh water for millions of people across the region.

title: North Window, Arches National Park, Moab, Utah, USA
caption: Info
subtitle: North Window, Arches National Park, Moab, Utah, USA
description:
Just north of Moab, Utah, the high-desert park is home to more than 2,000 natural sandstone arches—the densest concentration of arches in the world. Today's image, North Window, is one of the best-known formations in the park's Windows Section, where towering fins, openings and sculpted sandstone create a landscape that looks almost architectural.
North Window certainly has the look of a giant stone gateway, framing distant cliffs and ever-changing skies. But there was no blueprint, architect or construction crew involved. Instead, water, ice, temperature changes and gravity gradually wore away softer rock, leaving the tougher layers behind. This arch proves that nature can be one spectacular architect – with a very, very long construction schedule.

title: Abraham Lake in Alberta, Canada
caption: Info
subtitle: Abraham Lake in Alberta, Canada
description:
Dawn's first light is reflected on the frozen surface of Abraham Lake, framed by Rocky Mountains peaks in western Canada. In winter, this picturesque lake in Alberta is famous for its frozen bubbles of methane gas, trapped beneath the ice. Strong winds keep the surface clear of snow, offering winter-long views. Come spring, when the ice thaws, the gas escapes into the atmosphere.
Despite its natural beauty, the lake is a human-made reservoir, created in 1972 when the Bighorn Dam was built on the North Saskatchewan River. Its icy beauty in winter and turquoise waters in summer make it a popular photography spot all year round.

title: Victoria Harbour, Hong Kong, China
caption: Info
description: Welcome to Hong Kong, home to the world's largest collection of skyscrapers. Those pictured here tower above Victoria Harbour, whose deep waters allowed the island to develop as a busy trading port. Ships carrying tea, silk and other goods have passed through since the 1840s, but growth rocketed in the decades after World War II, fueling a construction boom. With little flat land available between the harbour and the hills, developers had to build upwards, creating this distinctive skyline. In 2026, Hong Kong has 569 buildings at least 150 metres tall high — more than any other city.
